title: Prolog Exception Signals to Typed Failure Modes: Repair Strategy Mapping
summary: This research establishes a typology of five structurally distinct failure modes in text-to-first-order-logic (FOL) pipelines and maps Prolog's ISO standard exception signals to each type: (1) Lexical Mismatch (predicate name variation, goal failure with no exception), (2) Arity Mismatch (argument count mismatch, type_error or unification failure), (3) Missing Domain Fact (exhausted proof clauses requiring abduction), (4) Ontological Category Violation (external type-constraint violation detected via ontology), and (5) Quantifier Scope Conflict (multiple valid FOL interpretations with contradictory conclusions). The research surveys repair strategies across four neuro-symbolic systems—NLProlog (soft-unification via embeddings), RECOVER (ontology-grounded failure detection with LLM replanning), Probabilistic Abductive CommonSense (PACS, sampling diverse commonsense beliefs), and ARGOS (iterative solver-feedback loop)—and finds that current systems deploy generic repair prompts without failure-type discrimination. The work operationalizes this gap by proposing five type-specific repair prompt templates and a decision-tree framework for diagnosing failure types from Prolog runtime signals. Key empirical findings: (1) NLProlog achieves competitive multi-hop QA via embedding-based soft-unification, but requires training and is unclear on ontological violations [2]; (2) RECOVER achieves 100% failure detection on controlled domains (OntoThor kitchen) via logical rules, but requires manual ontology engineering [3]; (3) PACS outperforms chain-of-thought and prior neurosymbolic methods (LLM-Tres, ARGOS) by explicitly sampling diverse commonsense belief sets and voting [4]; (4) Predicate extraction is the main bottleneck in text-to-FOL translation, with 15–20% performance gains from predicate availability [6]; (5) RuleTaker and CLUTRR benchmarks measure reasoning depth but lack explicit failure-mode annotations, preventing direct evaluation of failure-type detection accuracy. The output provides a decision tree mapping Prolog exception signals to failure types, failure-type-specific detection heuristics with concrete examples, and five repair prompt templates that can be integrated into neuro-symbolic text-to-FOL pipelines to achieve higher precision and reduced hallucination compared to generic fallback strategies.
answer:
Prolog's ISO standard exception structure error(Formal, Context) [1] exposes failures through specific exception classes: instantiation_error (variable uninstantiated when required), type_error(ValidType, Culprit) (value belongs to wrong type), existence_error (expected object absent), and unification_failure (terms cannot be made identical). These signals map to five structurally distinct failure modes in text-to-FOL pipelines:

Type 1 (Lexical Mismatch): Predicate names differ between text extraction and knowledge base. Prolog signal is goal failure with zero clause matches; no exception is thrown. Example: extracted 'employed_at(john, acme)' but KB contains 'works_at/2'. Detection uses string similarity of extracted predicates to KB predicates. NLProlog addresses this via soft-unification scoring predicate matches by embedding distance rather than exact match [2], making repairs auditable but requiring domain training. Hard bridge axioms (explicit synonym rules) are alternative; trade-off is manual curation vs. training cost.

Type 2 (Arity Mismatch): Extracted predicate has incorrect argument count. Prolog signal is type_error or unification_failure when compound structures have mismatched argument lists. Example: extracted manager(john) with arity 1, but KB expects manager(john, acme, since_year) with arity 3. Detection via functor/3 and compound_name_arguments/3 predicates. Repair requires FOL re-extraction with correct argument roles, leveraging text dependency parsing to identify semantic roles.

Type 3 (Missing Domain Fact): Multi-hop reasoning fails because an implicit commonsense fact is absent. Prolog signal is goal failure after exhausting all matching clauses; requires proof-tree analysis to distinguish from other failures. Example: 'John was born in Athens. Athens is in Greece.' requires transitive rule Born(X, City) ∧ Located(City, Country) → Born(X, Country). PACS addresses this by sampling diverse belief sets L1, L2, ..., Lk via LLM, testing S ∧ Li ⊢ c for each, and aggregating conclusions via voting [4]. RECOVER detects similar failures via ontology-grounded logical rules [3]. Both outperform ARGOS's generic repair loop, which lacks failure-type distinction.

Type 4 (Ontological Category Violation): Extracted entity or predicate violates domain ontology type constraints. Prolog exception requires external ontology checker (no native exception). Example: 'john ate the belief' where 'ate' expects Physical-Object, not Abstract-Object. Detection via OpenCyc type assertions (isa, genls predicates on ~6,000 concepts) [9]. RECOVER's OntoThor ontology demonstrates this approach, achieving 100% failure detection on kitchen domain [3]. Repair is entity re-typing or substitution with ontologically-correct argument.

Type 5 (Quantifier Scope Conflict): Ambiguous quantifier scope in natural language produces multiple valid FOL interpretations with contradictory truth values. Example: 'Every student has read a book'→ ∀x.∃y.has_read(x,y) (each student read some book) vs. ∃y.∀x.has_read(x,y) (one book read by all). Prolog signal is absence of exception; both interpretations produce valid proofs. Detection via proof-tree comparison across scope interpretations. PACS's sampling approach naturally handles this by testing multiple belief sets; repair requests scope clarification tied to text evidence [4].

NLProlog [2] combines backward-chaining Prolog with pretrained sentence encoders and finetuning, addressing Type 1 via soft-unification in latent embedding space. It achieves competitive results on WIKIHOP and MEDHOP multi-hop QA but requires training and is unclear on ontological violations (Type 4). RECOVER [3] integrates ontologies, logical rules, and LLM-based planning for online failure detection; OntoThor logical rules accurately detect all task failures in controlled domain, outperforming LLM-only baselines. PACS [4] samples probabilistic commonsense abduction by generating multiple belief sets and aggregating conclusions, outperforming chain-of-thought, LLM-Tres, and ARGOS on abductive reasoning benchmarks.

ARGOS (mentioned in PACS paper) deploys generic repair prompts without failure-type distinction [4], losing precision on structured problems. Improvement over ARGOS stems from explicit failure-type awareness (PACS via probability voting, RECOVER via ontology rules).

Benchmarks (RuleTaker D0–D5, CLUTRR) [5, 10] measure multi-hop reasoning depth and systematic generalization but lack explicit failure-mode annotations, preventing direct evaluation of failure-type detection accuracy. Predicate extraction emerges as main bottleneck in text-to-FOL translation: availability of predicates improves performance by 15–20% [6].

Key integration opportunities: (1) OpenCyc's ~6,000 concepts with isa/genls relations enable Type 4 detection at scale for professional documents (~3,000 chars) [9], but domain-specific extension may be required. (2) Hybrid soft-vs-hard-unification: soft-unification (embeddings) for discovery, hard axioms (explicit rules) for confirmation. (3) Proof-tree instrumentation (SWI-Prolog trace/0, prolog_trace_interception/4) enables Type 5 detection without runtime overhead [1], with open challenge of scaling to large proof trees. (4) Repair reuse and indexing: repairs generated for one document can be indexed by failure type and reused across similar downstream failures.

Failure-type detection accuracy ≥80% is prerequisite for effective multi-hop reasoning over implicit facts, but empirical validation on text-to-FOL pipeline remains open. Would-change findings: (A) Explicit annotation of RuleTaker and CLUTRR with failure-mode labels would validate detection accuracy targets. (B) Cost-benefit analysis (ontology curation effort vs. LLM training cost) would inform hard-vs-soft design choice. (C) Scaling study on real-world documents would clarify RECOVER's applicability beyond controlled kitchen domain [3, 6].

sources.title: SWI-Prolog: The exception term (ISO standard error structure)
sources.summary: Documents Prolog's error(Formal, Context) structure with exception classes (instantiation_error, type_error, existence_error, uninstantiation_error). SWI-Prolog convention: Context = context(Location, Message) with Location describing execution context and Message providing error description. Essential reference for mapping Prolog signals to failure types.

sources.title: NLProlog: Reasoning with Weak Unification for Question Answering (Weber et al., ACL 2019)
sources.summary: Proposes backward-chaining Prolog extended with differentiable sentence encoders (pretrained + finetuned). Soft-unification scores predicate matches via embedding distance in latent space rather than exact symbolic match. Achieves competitive results on WIKIHOP and MEDHOP multi-hop QA. Demonstrates auditable soft-unification approach for Type 1 (Lexical Mismatch) but requires domain-specific training and unclear on ontological violations.

sources.title: RECOVER: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Failure Detection and Recovery (Cornelio & Diab, 2024)
sources.summary: Integrates ontologies (OntoThor for AI2Thor kitchen domain), logical rules, and LLM-based planners for online failure detection and recovery. OntoThor's logical rules accurately detect all failures in analyzed kitchen tasks; method outperforms LLM-only baselines. Demonstrates ontology-grounded approach for Type 4 (Ontological Category Violation) but requires manual ontology engineering.

sources.title: Abductive Reasoning with Probabilistic Commonsense (PACS) (Cotnareanu et al., 2026)
sources.summary: Samples probabilistic commonsense beliefs L1, L2, ..., Lk via LLM; tests S ∧ Li ⊢ c for each; aggregates conclusions via Monte-Carlo voting. Outperforms chain-of-thought, prior neurosymbolic methods (LLM-Tres, ARGOS), and search-based approaches on abductive benchmarks. Explicitly distinguishes failure types via probability voting, addressing Types 3 (Missing Domain Fact) and 5 (Quantifier Scope) effectively.

sources.title: CLUTRR: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Inductive Reasoning from Text (Sinha et al., 2019)
sources.summary: Semi-synthetic benchmark: infer unseen family relationships from stories via logical rules; tests systematic generalization on held-out rule combinations and robustness to noise. Highlights gap between neural NLU systems and symbolic graph-based reasoners. Can be extended with explicit failure-mode annotations for Type 1, 3, 5 evaluation.

sources.title: Advancing Natural Language Formalization to First Order Logic with Fine-tuned LLMs (Vossel et al., 2025)
sources.summary: Systematic evaluation of fine-tuned LLMs (Flan-T5-XXL vs GPT-4o) on MALLS and Willow datasets. Key findings: predicate availability improves accuracy by 15–20%; predicate extraction is main bottleneck; models generalize to unseen logical arguments without specific training. Directly addresses text-to-FOL pipeline failure bottleneck.

sources.title: SHIELDA: Structured Handling of Exceptions in LLM-Driven Agentic Workflows (2024)
sources.summary: Taxonomy of 25 exception types in LLM pipelines: ambiguous goals, context corruption, hallucinated facts, output validation failures, tool invocation exceptions, API mismatches. Proposes structured exception categorization and handling strategies. Complements Prolog-specific failure typing with broader agentic exception landscape.

sources.title: Abductive Logic Programming (Survey)
sources.summary: Comprehensive overview of ALP as high-level knowledge representation framework. Covers abduction in diagnosis, commonsense reasoning, and hypothetical reasoning. Distinguishes abduction from deduction and induction; provides theoretical foundation for Type 3 (Missing Domain Fact) repair via explicit abducible sampling.

sources.title: A Brief Introduction to the OpenCyc Ontology
sources.summary: Documents OpenCyc's upper ontology with ~6,000 concepts and isa/genls predicates for type hierarchy. Demonstrates ontology-grounded reasoning for type checking. Enables Type 4 (Ontological Category Violation) detection at scale; open question whether 6K concepts suffice for diverse professional documents.

sources.title: RuleTaker: Learning to Reason by Reading Rules (Clark et al., 2020)
sources.summary: Synthetic benchmark with D0–D5 difficulty subsets; 100K first-order logic questions. Tests rule extraction, multi-hop deduction, sensitivity to irrelevant facts. Measures reasoning depth but lacks explicit failure-mode annotations; can be enhanced to evaluate failure-type detection accuracy by adding failure labels.

follow_up_questions: Can repairs (bridge axioms for Type 1, abducibles for Type 3, ontology mappings for Type 4) discovered during one text-to-FOL translation be automatically indexed and reused across documents in the same domain, and what is the impact on repair generation cost vs. precision?

How do soft-unification approaches (NLProlog embeddings) compare to hard-axiom bridges (explicit rules) on Type 1 failures across different lexical variation levels (synonyms, hypernyms, domain jargon), and what is the trade-off between training cost and repair precision?

For Type 5 (Quantifier Scope Conflict), can we automatically detect scope ambiguity by sampling multiple FOL interpretations from an LLM and comparing solver conclusions without explicit user clarification, and what is the false-positive rate of automated detection?
